arguments.name: Tamsin
arguments.attitude: Wary but practical. She'll take company on the road and isn't offering any favours.

relation.note: Agreed to share the moor road to Hollin Ford on her terms: walk at the back, carry your own food, and stay on Bran's good side.

arguments.statblock: Commoner drover. Hazel stick 1d4. Dog Bran: alert, warns of strangers and predators, herds on command.

identity.observableVoice: Short, dry and plain-spoken. Counts things on her fingers and talks while she works. Wary of strangers without being hostile.

arguments.name: Hollin Ford
arguments.description: A market town two days east of the wayside square, over the moor road. It's market week, and hands are reportedly wanted for penning and tallying.

arguments.value: Tamsin leaves east on the moor road once the flock has drunk. She does not wait. If Rowan isn't ready, they must catch up on the road (easy within the first hour).
arguments.warning: She said she's off once the ewes have drunk their fill.
arguments.consequence: Tamsin and the flock set out on the moor road toward Hollin Ford with or without Rowan.

arguments.value: Market week at Hollin Ford; the main sheep market is on day 3. Daily-paid penning/tallying work is available. Rowan has no food and no money, which matters for Tamsin's 'carry your own food' term.

result.summary: 10 minutes pass (Talking with Tamsin at the trough while the flock drinks)

narration:
Tamsin is easy to pick out. She looks about eighteen, sleeves rolled to the elbow, and she's working two dozen grey-faced ewes around the water trough with a hazel stick and a low whistle. At each whistle a black-and-white dog slips along the flock's flank. When you ask, she looks you over the way a buyer looks over a ram: boots first, then your hands, then the compass at your belt.

"If by 'same way' you mean east over the moor road, then you mean Hollin Ford. Two days with this lot, if they don't sulk." She whistles once and the dog drops flat in the dust. "Tamsin. You can walk with me. Company's no bad thing up on the tops."

Then she counts her terms off on her fingers.

"You walk at the back and you mind the stragglers. You don't mind me. You carry your own food, because I've none to spare. And if Bran takes against you, you walk a mile behind and there's no hard feelings."

For now the dog just watches you with its chin on its paws.

"I'm off once they've drunk their fill. I won't wait past that." She tips her head toward the notice board, where the work organiser is pinning up a fresh sheet. "It's market week at the Ford. They always want hands for penning and tallying. If it's work you're after, that's where it'll be. I can't pay you in anything but conversation."

A ewe shoves another out of the trough. Tamsin is already moving to break it up.

input: Tamsin, why are you really on this road? You don't look like someone chasing herd money.

narration:
Tamsin doesn't answer straight off. She hooks the shoving ewe round the neck with the crook of her stick and steers it to the far end of the trough. Only then does she look back at you, boots first again, as if checking she got it right the first time.

"Herd money's exactly what I'm chasing." She wipes her palm on her breeches. "What did you think it'd look like? Fat man on a cob with a purse on his belt?"

She turns back to the flock and counts heads under her breath, her lips moving. *Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four.*

"Most years Dad takes them over." She leaves a pause just long enough to notice. "This year it's me. That's the whole of it, and it's more than I'd tell most folk at a trough." She doesn't say it sharply. She says it the way she'd remark on rain coming. "And that's one of my terms, by the way. You don't mind me."

While she talks, the dog gets up. Bran circles wide around the flock and comes in low. He sniffs your boots, then your empty hands, then the compass case. He sits down a yard off with his head tilted and doesn't settle either way.

Tamsin watches him do it, then looks at you properly for the first time.

"My turn, then. You've good boots, a compass and no pack. Not so much as a heel of bread on you." Half the ewes have already lifted their dripping muzzles from the water. "So what road are *you* on?"

input: Tamsin, if it goes bad at the coast, what do you want me to do?

arguments.value: Rowan asked Tamsin about things 'going bad at the coast'. No coast is established on the moor road. Tamsin has never seen the sea and has no idea where it lies. Possible hook for Rowan's own goal if the player builds on it.

result.summary: 5 minutes pass (Talking at the trough while the last ewes drink)

narration:
Tamsin's hand stops halfway to her stick.

"The coast." She says it flat, the way she'd repeat a price that was too high. "There's no coast on this road. It's moor, then the Ford, then more moor on the far side. I've never seen the sea, and this road won't show it you."

She looks at you a moment longer, then snorts. It isn't unkind.

"That's twice I've asked what road you're on, and twice you've answered something else. I'll take that as an answer of a kind." She hooks a dawdling ewe away from the trough. "If the coast's where you're bound, that's your business. I'm not going there, and I'll not promise you anything about it."

She counts on her fingers again. The list is shorter this time.

"What I want if it goes bad up on the tops, though, I'll tell you. If fog comes down, you stop where you are and you shout. You don't go looking for me. If something gets at the flock, you keep out of Bran's way and keep the stragglers bunched. And if you go lame, I'll send someone back from the Ford. I won't turn twenty-four ewes round for you." A beat. "Wouldn't for anyone."

Most of the ewes have lifted their heads from the water now. Bran is on his feet before anyone tells him. He's watching her, not you.

"Nearly time," she says, and moves to the head of the flock.
